title: The backend contract: files are not necessarily a filesystem
kicker: Start with capabilities, not storage names
summary: Understand structured file data, result envelopes, pagination, exact edits, optional execution, and the sync/async bridges that every backend consumer relies on.

sections.title: A storage interface, with execution as a separate capability
sections.body:
A backend answers a narrow question: where do the harness’s file operations go? A file may live in graph state, a LangGraph store namespace, a host filesystem, or a remote execution provider. Storage capability does not imply a shell.

A capability is an operation a backend can actually perform, not a guarantee about where or how safely it runs. To read /notes/brief.txt and write /notes/report.txt, the agent needs file capabilities. Running a report-generation command additionally requires execution capability; choosing storage alone does not grant it.

The capability contract

  • File operations are the shared vocabulary. Backends expose listing, reading, writing, editing, deleting, literal searching, globbing, and byte transfer. StateBackend and StoreBackend can search documents entirely in Python without owning an operating-system process.
  • Inheritance is not a completeness check. BackendProtocol is an abstract-base-class-shaped interface. Ordinary operation methods default to NotImplementedError, but deliberately are not all abstract methods: partial implementations can be instantiated. Deletion is explicitly optional; its support helper compares the concrete class’s delete with the base implementation. Implement every operation your consumers expose.
  • Execution is an additional capability, not an isolation certificate. SandboxBackendProtocol adds an id and execute/aexecute. The unrestricted host-backed LocalShellBackend implements it too. Public package exports collect state, store, composite, disk, local-shell, LangSmith, and Context Hub backends; fuller result and sandbox types live in implementation modules.

Choose authority first: decide whether the agent should possess execution before selecting a backend. Do not teach shell fallbacks for file-only backends. Conversely, shell commands do not automatically inherit structured file tools’ permission checks or literal-search result contract.

sections.title: FileData and the different kinds of failure
sections.body:
A successful backend read returns a result envelope: a record containing the payload and metadata about the operation. The payload is FileData, not yet the numbered text the model sees. Its content is always a string: ordinary text uses encoding="utf-8"; arbitrary binary bytes can be represented as a base64 string.

Start with one successful read

Illustrative record, not executed: suppose /notes/brief.txt contains exactly Goal: summarize\nAudience: developers\n. A full text read can produce the following record; optional timestamps are omitted here.

ReadResult(
    file_data={
        "content": "Goal: summarize\nAudience: developers\n",
        "encoding": "utf-8",
    },
    total_lines=2,
    start_line=1,
    end_line=2,
    next_offset=None,
    error=None,
)

First check error, then interpret file_data using its encoding. Here the range covers both source lines and next_offset=None means no remaining page.

Read that same brief one line at a time

  1. Request offset 0, limit 1. The payload is Goal: summarize\n, with total_lines=2, start_line=1, end_line=1, and next_offset=1.
  2. Resume at offset 1, limit 1. The payload is Audience: developers\n, with source range 2–2 and next_offset=None. The windows changed; the stored file did not. The next section explains the zero-based offset and one-based line-number relationship.

Other results and failure channels

Operation familyResult dataWhat to inspect
readReadResult.file_data and pagination fieldserror first, then encoding and window metadata
write / edit / deletepath; edit also reports occurrencesHuman-readable error, not a standardized exception code
ls / grep / globStructured entries or matchesErrors and incompleteness, not just whether a list is empty
upload / downloadOne response per requested input; downloads contain bytesPer-item error, preserving correlation and partial success
  • Timestamps distinguish inspection from mutation. FileData has optional creation and modification timestamps. Helpers create UTC ISO strings. Updating preserves a present creation timestamp, retains encoding unless the caller changes it, and advances modification time. Reading a slice instead copies timestamps unchanged: inspection is not mutation.
  • Transfer errors are per item, not one batch verdict. The four named errors are file_not_found, permission_denied, is_directory, and invalid_path. Backend-specific strings are also permitted, so authentication or transport failures need not fit those four categories. Do not collapse failures into “missing file” or infer batch success from the first item.
  • Result envelopes do not suppress every exception. Each backend chooses what to translate. Store conversion, for example, rejects unsupported content types; provider adapters differ in whether transfer exceptions are caught per file. Direct callers need both result handling and an exception policy appropriate to their chosen backend.

sources.label: Successful text read and page-window metadata

sections.title: Pagination is a source-line contract, not display formatting
sections.body:
Read offsets are zero-based; reported source-line numbers are one-based. Pagination describes source text, not the line-number gutters added by filesystem middleware. Gutters never become stored file contents.

Follow a page window

Illustrative trace, not executed: assume /notes/brief.txt contains six lines, one two three four five six. The last line deliberately has no final newline.

  1. Request the middle page. read("/notes/brief.txt", offset=2, limit=2) skips two source lines. Its payload content is three four , with total_lines=6, start_line=3, end_line=4, and next_offset=4.
  2. Resume using the returned offset unchanged. A second call with offset=4, limit=2 returns five six, source lines 5–6, and next_offset=None. Adding one to the resume offset would incorrectly skip line 5.
  3. Let middleware format the page afterward. Display gutters can identify lines 3 and 4, but the backend payload contains only their source text. An edit should match that text, not copied gutter characters.

How the shared slicer handles boundaries

  • Clamp the requested window and handle empty content. Negative offsets and limits become zero. Empty or whitespace-only content gets its special empty-content behavior before the zero-limit branch. For nonblank text, zero limit returns an empty payload with no_lines_requested=True: no window was inspected, not an empty file.
  • Slice source lines without inventing a final newline. The slicer uses splitlines(keepends=True), preserving whether the last line had a terminator. Within the returned window it normalizes CRLF and CR to LF. An offset at or beyond the available nonblank lines returns an error.
  • Report the next starting position. A real page has start_line=offset+1 and end_line equal to its last returned source line. When more lines remain, next_offset=end_line. This already is the next zero-based position; do not increment it again.
ReadResult invariants and nontext reads

ReadResult.__post_init__ makes malformed pagination fail visibly: start and end must appear together, the range must run forward, total lines cannot be smaller than its end, and a resume offset must equal the end-line number. An uninspected-window flag cannot coexist with errors or pagination metadata.

Binary and media-oriented reads may bypass slicing; inspect encoding and backend behavior before assuming text pagination.

sections.title: Exact replacement and search completeness
sections.body:
Edits are exact substring replacements, not fuzzy patches. Search has an equally important distinction: no matches and incomplete evidence are different outcomes.

How an exact edit is accepted

  1. Validate the old string and count matches. The shared helper rejects an empty old string and errors when no occurrence exists. Several occurrences with replace_all false require unique surrounding context. Once accepted, Python string replacement performs the edit and the result reports the count. State and store reject text edits of base64 files.
  2. Keep trailing-newline differences explicit. If the old string ends in a newline but the file ends in its unterminated form, the helper does not relax the match. It returns a targeted explanation. If the stripped form is also ambiguous, the message requests both removal of the trailing newline and additional context. Read-time newline preservation therefore affects edit correctness.

Read search results in two parts

  1. Inspect completeness before interpreting absence. GrepResult can contain valid matches alongside an error and has a separate truncated flag. GlobResult also distinguishes budget exhaustion, unreadable subtrees, and clipped transport. Narrower patterns can help a budget-limited walk, but cannot grant access to unreadable subtrees. A single backend’s grep cap is total across files; exactly reaching it is complete unless another match was dropped.
  2. Use this glob contract, not shell assumptions. Slash-free patterns match basenames at any depth; slash-containing patterns match relative paths; a leading slash anchors to the search root. A bare *.yml can find a normal basename inside a dot-directory, while **/*.yml does not descend through dot-directory segments. Classic shell globbing and plain fnmatch are not interchangeable substitutes.

sections.title: Async convenience does not imply cancellation of work
sections.body:
The base interface bridges many async methods with asyncio.to_thread. A synchronous backend can participate in an async graph without directly blocking the event loop, but that does not create a new storage engine or make its work cancellable.

Separate three async mechanisms

  1. A caller timeout need not stop work. Standard agrep wraps its thread call in an async timeout. Expiry bounds the caller’s wait, not the worker thread’s lifetime. A slow operation can continue consuming resources after a timeout result has reached its caller.
  2. Signature compatibility changes where limits apply. Grep introspection detects max_count. Modern implementations receive the cap during search; older signatures run first and are trimmed afterward. Both return bounded lists, but only the former can avoid materializing uncapped results. Execution’s timeout-support probe similarly inspects and caches the concrete execute signature; direct protocol-level async execution forwards an explicit timeout only if supported.
  3. Native overrides can own real async transports. Store reads/writes call aget/aput. BaseSandbox async file helpers call aexecute, letting providers centralize native async transport. LangSmith caches a client belonging to its creating event loop and provides aclose to release the pool. Reuse across unrelated loops is unsupported.

When debugging hangs: distinguish backend command timeout, outer caller deadline, transport timeout, and surviving local threads. They have different cleanup guarantees; one expiring does not prove the others stopped.

title: State, store, and durable lifetimes
summary: Trace graph-channel writes and reducers, understand namespace isolation and store costs, and separate checkpoint restoration from external side-effect rollback.

sections.title: StateBackend reads the current graph, not an instance-owned dictionary
sections.body:
Ask two separate questions about a file: which identity selects it, and what storage keeps it alive? Reusing a Python backend instance answers neither. State files follow graph execution; store files follow a namespace in the selected store.

A thread is the conversation identity used to resume graph state. A checkpoint is a saved graph-state position; a checkpointer saves and retrieves those positions. A store namespace is a tuple of strings grouping keys, such as ("user-42", "filesystem"). A namespace is not automatically a thread or an authorization rule.

BackendWhat selects /notes/brief.txt?What must survive?
StateBackendThe active thread’s files graph channelIts saved state, through the configured checkpointer when resuming runs
StoreBackendThe namespace factory’s tuple plus the file-path keyThe selected store’s data and the same namespace mapping

Follow one file through three lifetimes

Illustrative trace, not executed: thread A writes /notes/brief.txt. Compare a state-backed version with a store-backed version using namespace ("user-42", "filesystem"). Assume later reads do not overwrite or delete the file.

  1. Continue thread A. A later graph invocation can read the state version if it resumes the saved thread state through its checkpointer. The store version is available when it resolves the same namespace against the same retained store data.
  2. Start an independent thread B. With no copied initial files, B does not inherit A’s state file. B can read the store version if its trusted namespace factory returns the same tuple. A different namespace selects different keys even when the path string is identical.
  3. Restart the application process. A’s state version is recoverable only if checkpoint data survives and the application reconnects to it with the appropriate thread/configuration. The store version requires retained store data and the same namespace. Fresh in-memory checkpointer/store instances do not manufacture restart durability.

How StateBackend writes within a running graph

StateBackend() owns no files dictionary. Each operation resolves the active LangGraph configuration and requires its internal read/send hooks. One instance follows the current graph task instead of capturing one conversation’s snapshot. A superstep is a graph execution round whose task writes are applied at its boundary.

  1. Read the current graph view. Resolve configuration and call read("files", fresh=True). Fresh reads apply pending task writes through the files reducer, so a tool can write and immediately read or edit a file within the same superstep.
  2. Build only the changed file data. Create or update one FileData, preserving creation metadata on overwrite. Mutation supplies a partial dictionary, not a replacement for the entire filesystem.
  3. Queue the channel update. Send {path: file_data} to the files channel. The send queues task writes; the node boundary commits them to graph state. Callers do not extract a separate “files update” from the result and merge it themselves.
  4. Return the path and allow a fresh reread. Return WriteResult(path=...). Subsequent fresh reads see the queued value even before the node boundary.

Illustrative in-tool trace: write /notes/brief.txt with “first,” edit “first” to “revised,” then read it. Fresh reads make the edit find the newly queued file.

Outside a graph: the same sequence fails at configuration lookup with a clear runtime error; it does not create an object-local filesystem. Supply initial files through graph invocation input instead of writing directly before execution.

sources.label: Store and namespace selection per operation

sections.title: Merging files, deletions, and checkpoint scope
sections.body:
The filesystem state schema uses a DeltaChannel: it records file changes and periodically materializes a snapshot to bound the work needed to reconstruct the channel. Here snapshot_frequency=50 means snapshots about every 50 Pregel steps. It is not a 50-step retention limit, a file expiry setting, or a promise of durable storage.

How state changes combine

  • The reducer merges keys, not competing text edits. A reducer is the function combining channel updates. This one copies the prior dictionary once, applies step writes in order, overwrites named keys, and treats None as deletion. Unrelated file updates preserve one another. Several writes to one key follow the supplied sequence; there is no semantic conflict-resolution algorithm merging different edits.
  • Deletion respects a path-component boundary. State deletion strips a trailing slash, matches the exact key and keys starting with that base plus a slash, then sends tombstones. Deleting /work includes /work/a.txt, not /workspace/a.txt. Flat state can contain an exact file key and nested keys simultaneously; listings synthesize apparent directories from prefixes, not inodes.
  • “Ephemeral” is not “one tool call.” A supplied LangGraph checkpointer can retain thread state between runs. Without durable checkpoint storage, the backend itself supplies no disk durability. The SDK passes checkpointer and store separately: checkpoints concern graph state; stores concern external shared data. They are not interchangeable memory mechanisms.

External effects are not graph deltas: restoring graph state does not promise to undo writes to a separate store, host filesystem, Hub repository, or sandbox. For example, rewinding the graph after writing a host-backed /notes/report.txt does not restore that file’s previous bytes. Plan side-effect idempotency and cleanup at the application boundary.

sources.label: Store effects are immediate adapter calls

sections.title: StoreBackend namespace resolution is the isolation seam
sections.body:
StoreBackend requires a namespace factory. Namespace selection is the isolation seam: different threads intentionally share files when they resolve to the same namespace, not merely because they use the same backend class.

Read the storage contract in four parts

  1. Resolve identity on every operation. Each operation obtains a runtime and calls the factory, allowing a user identity plus an application-specific “filesystem” component. Inject the store explicitly or obtain it from active graph execution. Outside a graph, an explicit store and constant factory work with runtime None; dereferencing unavailable runtime produces a clarified runtime error.
  2. Validate namespace syntax, then establish authorization separately. The validator rejects an empty tuple, non-string or empty components, and characters outside ASCII alphanumerics plus hyphen, underscore, dot, at-sign, plus, colon, and tilde. Wildcards are forbidden to prevent lookup expansion. These checks do not authorize users: derive identity from trusted runtime context, not an agent-controlled identifier that could select another tenant.
  3. Treat paths as store keys. Reads use store.get(namespace, file_path). Writes read the old value for metadata, build FileData, then call put. Edits similarly read, check exact occurrences, and write. No compare-and-swap or transaction spans that read-modify-write; concurrent editors can overwrite accepted updates unless the store or application adds stronger coordination.
  4. Choose durability explicitly. “Persistent, cross-thread” names the storage seam, not a guarantee that every BaseStore survives restart. Tests use InMemoryStore; the adapter does not manufacture durable media. Durable cross-conversation memory needs an appropriate store implementation and stable namespace.

sections.title: Listing, scanning, legacy data, and binary round-trips
sections.body:
Backend names do not determine lifetime or cost. Check the actual storage implementation, namespace, resource, and conversion path.

Three store behaviors to budget for

  1. Small directory requests can scan large namespaces. Listing searches the namespace in pages of 100 until an empty or short page, materializes items, then filters prefixes locally. This avoids dependence on a store’s filtering semantics, but broad listing/search cost scales with namespace size even for a small directory. Async pagination uses the native async search API.
  2. Legacy data conversion can fail differently from absence. Old list[str] content is joined without mutating the stored item; missing encoding defaults to UTF-8; only string timestamps survive conversion. Unsupported content types raise TypeError, absent content raises ValueError. Some read/edit paths translate the latter into result errors, but do not universally catch the former. Corrupt schema is not simply a missing file.
  3. Byte transfer and text mutation follow different encoding rules. Uploads try UTF-8, base64-encode undecodable bytes, and store fresh file data; downloads decode using stored encoding. Ordinary text writes force UTF-8 even over binary entries. Binary text edits are rejected. State/store binary-grep tests assert that binary payloads neither appear as matches nor consume the match budget.
Where bytes liveWhat provides lifetimePrimary diagnostic
StateBackendThread state; configured checkpointer for retention across runsCorrect thread and graph context?
StoreBackendChosen store implementation and namespaceSame trusted namespace and durable store?
FilesystemBackendHost filesystem or mounted volumeCorrect root and process permissions?
Remote sandboxProvider resource lifetime and volumesSame resource ID, still alive?
ContextHubBackendHub commits plus adapter cacheCommit accepted, cache refreshed after conflict?

title: Host filesystem access and the shell boundary
kicker: Virtual paths are not process isolation
summary: Follow real-path resolution, symlink checks, permanent mutations, search fallback, and the unrestricted subprocess behavior of LocalShellBackend.

sections.title: How a virtual path reaches a host file
sections.body:
FilesystemBackend exposes real disk files through backend paths. In its default virtual mode, a leading slash means “from the configured backend root,” not “from the host’s filesystem root.” The root is the resolved supplied directory, or the process working directory if none is supplied.

Map a normal file before considering aliases

Illustrative mapping, not executed: configure FilesystemBackend(root_dir="/srv/work"). Assume that root and its notes directory are ordinary directories, not symlinks.

Backend pathResolved host pathMeaning
/notes/brief.txt/srv/work/notes/brief.txtRead the brief under the application root
notes/brief.txt/srv/work/notes/brief.txtThe resolver supplies the leading virtual slash
/notes/report.txt/srv/work/notes/report.txtA write creates or overwrites a real host file

How virtual resolution works

  1. Normalize and reject traversal-like input. The resolver adds a leading slash when absent and rejects the substring ... This is stricter than middleware’s component-based validation: a filename containing two dots can pass virtual path validation but fail this resolver.
  2. Resolve symlinks and verify containment. The joined path is resolved through symlinks and checked to remain relative to the root. Symlink loops are explicitly checked. An absolute-looking virtual input cannot simply bypass the root.
  3. Keep layer-specific input rules in view. Middleware rejects a leading tilde before normalization; the disk resolver prepends a slash before its own leading-tilde test. These layers do not necessarily accept identical inputs. Read their actual code rather than generalizing from documentation.

Nonvirtual mode changes the authority. Absolute paths are host paths; relative paths resolve against the backend’s configured working directory. The root is a convenience base, not confinement. Relative traversal or absolute host paths can reach outside it; use this mode only when that authority is intentional.

Permission coordinates: _real_path exposes symlink-resolved paths: virtual coordinates in virtual mode, host-root-relative coordinates otherwise. Middleware recursively applies this through composite mounts, so requested and resolved targets can both be checked.

Not race-free isolation: resolution and opening are separate. Validation and O_NOFOLLOW are guardrails, not OS-level protection against hostile concurrent filesystem modification.

sections.title: Reading and mutating real bytes
sections.body:
A host-backed write changes real bytes immediately; it is not a graph-state delta. A line-window request does not imply a window-sized disk read, and a result error does not promise that no external change occurred.

Follow the report’s host effects

Illustrative trace, not executed: with root /srv/work and ordinary directories, read /notes/brief.txt, then write /notes/report.txt with “Draft.” The write changes /srv/work/notes/report.txt. Restoring an older graph checkpoint does not restore that file’s previous contents.

If you then delete /notes/report.txt successfully, that host file is unlinked; the brief remains. Deleting the directory /notes instead recursively removes both files and other contents. Neither operation means “remove this only from the model’s context.” A later host read sees the resulting filesystem, not a checkpoint’s earlier view.

Read each operation’s effects separately

  • Reads load text before pagination. The backend resolves the path, verifies a regular file, and opens with O_NOFOLLOW where available. Extensions select base64 binary content or UTF-8 text; video has a dedicated size guard. Ordinary text is read before shared slicing, so small windows need not reduce memory proportionally. Empty/whitespace-only files get an empty-content reminder; decoding failures become read-result errors.
  • Writes overwrite existing files. Parent directories are created, then create-and-truncate flags open the destination. UTF-8 is written with newline translation disabled. The effect is a host write, not a graph-state update that checkpoint restoration can undo.
  • Edits can normalize the whole file. The backend reads the entire file with universal-newline conversion, normalizes old/new strings to LF, applies exact replacement, then truncates and rewrites. An entire CRLF file can become LF. Unlike the remote sandbox helper, it does not try to preserve the first matching line-ending style. Read-modify-write is not an atomic patch transaction.
  • Deletion follows the resolved path. It unlinks a leaf or recursively removes a directory. Although there is an explicit symlink-unlink branch, virtual resolution may already have followed the link to its target. Do not generalize the docstring’s “remove only the link” claim to every virtual alias. Middleware checks resolved targets; direct backend calls lack that protection.

Partial deletion is possible: directory removal may delete entries before a permission failure. An error is not evidence of no change. Use disposable workspaces or isolated volumes for experiments with agent-generated modifications.

Remote deletion: shell quoting is not root confinement either

BaseSandbox.delete probes existence, then passes a quoted literal path to rm -rf. Quoting prevents metacharacters splitting the argument; it does not confine deletion to an application root. Whatever the sandbox shell can reach remains within its deletion authority.

A nonzero existence probe can mean absent or unstatable. An unknown probe exit falls through rather than inventing a not-found diagnosis. Recursive removal can also partly succeed before an error. These are backend-specific filesystem effects, separate from execution-output capture.

sections.title: Literal search, fallback engines, and partial evidence
sections.body:
Disk grep prefers ripgrep but can fall back to Python. An empty match list is not universal evidence that the requested path was successfully searched.

Trace the search before broadening it

  1. Validate input and choose an engine. Grep validates its include glob, resolves the search base, and tries ripgrep literal matching. If that cannot provide results, Python scans literal substrings. Nonexistent or traversal-rejected paths can yield an empty list instead of the read operation’s error shape.
  2. Check fallback-specific limits. Python scanning has a configurable file-size ceiling, default 10 MiB. Large files can be skipped; this is not a global size limit for every operation. Direct-backend grep also accepts context_lines, which the agent-facing schema intentionally does not expose.
  3. Keep useful matches and partial errors together. If matching files cannot be reread for context, grep can return matches plus an error. Diagnostics should preserve both rather than discard valid matches or claim complete evidence.
  4. Distinguish phase budgets from cancellation. Sync grep phases and the async wrapper have separate timeouts; the async default leaves room for ripgrep followed by Python fallback. That wait budget does not cancel worker threads. Diagnose resolution, glob syntax, preferred-engine failure, fallback limits, or context rereading first: broadening a timed-out query usually adds work.

sections.title: LocalShellBackend crosses to unrestricted host execution
sections.body:
LocalShellBackend combines disk tools with execution. root_dir sets the subprocess working directory; virtual_mode governs only structured file operations. Commands retain the operating-system user’s authority over accessible host paths, parent directories, network connections, and other programs.

Read the execution contract in three parts

  1. Construction sets timeout and environment, not confinement. A positive default timeout is required, normally 120 seconds, and a local resource ID is generated. The command environment is empty unless supplied; inherit_env copies the parent environment and overlays supplied values. This reduces accidental inheritance, but accessible credentials on disk or other host resources remain accessible.
  2. Execution invokes a real shell. The command string goes directly to subprocess.run(shell=True). Stdout/stderr are captured, stdin is DEVNULL, and non-Windows processes start a new session. Stderr lines are prefixed in combined output. An explicit environment may lack search paths or application settings, explaining differences from an interactive terminal.
  3. Output limits apply after capture. Only after the process returns is combined output encoded and clipped to the configured byte limit. A small returned budget does not bound captured memory. Ordinary nonzero command exits are execution responses with exit codes, not Python exceptions.

No validator makes this a sandbox: a working directory is not a chroot; an empty environment is not a container; a timeout is not rollback. Implementing SandboxBackendProtocol does not certify isolation. Untrusted commands require a genuinely constrained environment and explicit approval policy.

title: CompositeBackend: a virtual mount table
kicker: Routing storage does not route shell commands
summary: Work through longest-prefix dispatch, mount roots, path rewriting, cross-backend searches and transfers, and the execution/default distinction.

sections.title: Longest matching mount wins, then the prefix disappears
sections.body:
A composite backend owns a default backend and virtual route-prefix dictionary. Routes select destinations; their names do not automatically create storage namespaces.

How a path is dispatched

  1. Try the longest route first. Routes are sorted by descending prefix length. A match is either the route root without its trailing slash or a path beginning with a component-delimited route prefix. Similar-looking sibling names do not match that prefix.
  2. Remove the mount prefix. A matched root becomes /; a descendant becomes its suffix with one leading slash. Unmatched paths pass to the default unchanged. Successful mutations restore the original external path in their result, so the model keeps using the mount name rather than the backend-local key.
Illustrative inputRoutesSelected target
/memories/memories/memory backend, /
/memories/a.txt/memories/memory backend, /a.txt
/memories-private/a.txt/memories/default, unchanged path
/memories/team/a.txt/memories/ and /memories/team/team backend, /a.txt

This table illustrates the routing algorithm; it is not executed output. Routed disk backends normally need virtual mode: their received /a.txt should be beneath the configured root, not at the host root.

Aliasing trap: if /memories/ and /cache/ point to the same store backend and namespace, /memories/a.txt and /cache/a.txt both become key /a.txt. Route names are not namespace components.

Trusted configuration: the constructor documents slash conventions but simply stores the supplied dictionary and sorted entries. Treat route configuration as application wiring.

sections.title: Root listing and cross-backend searches are different operations
sections.body:
A root listing, a routed search, and an aggregate search do different work. Composite mounts are routing rules, not a physical filesystem union. The path you supply determines whether the operation reaches one backend or several.

Distinguish three search scopes

Illustrative trace, not executed: use a default backend with mounts declared in this order: /memories/, then /archive/. Neither mount matches /notes.

CallWork performed
grep("TODO", path="/notes")Default only, with /notes unchanged; no mounted store is searched
grep("TODO", path="/memories")Memory backend only, with backend-local root /
grep("TODO", path="/") or omitted pathDefault first, then routed backends in route declaration order

Follow an aggregate match budget

For grep("TODO", path="/", max_count=3), suppose the default contributes two matches and memory contributes one. These are assumed inputs to the following trace, not measured search results.

  1. Spend two matches on the default. The default receives cap 3 and returns two matches. Two of the three available slots are now occupied.
  2. Pass only the remaining budget to memory. The /memories/ backend receives cap 1 at its local root. Its one match at /brief.txt is returned as /memories/brief.txt.
  3. Skip archive once no budget remains. The aggregate returns three matches and truncated=True. Archive was not inspected. Even if archive actually contains no matches, the flag conservatively reports incomplete coverage.

Longest-prefix sorting chooses the backend for a particular path. It does not sort root-search fanout: the implementation iterates the original route dictionary after searching the default. Aggregate matches are not globally ranked.

Listing, errors, and other aggregation details

  • Listing a mount stays within that backend. Child paths are rewritten beneath the route prefix. Listing / instead asks the default for root entries, appends virtual route directories, and sorts; it does not recursively list every mounted store. A default-listing failure is surfaced rather than presenting mount directories as the whole world.
  • One match budget covers the aggregate. Each subsequent route receives the remaining cap. At zero, later routes are skipped and truncation is reported. Exactly filling the budget can mark the result incomplete even if skipped routes would add nothing. Check whether an earlier backend consumed the budget when a match seems missing.
  • Errors remain aggregate failures. A route error short-circuits instead of becoming default-only success. Glob merging sorts paths, combines truncation state, and remaps every routed match. A healthy backend’s result does not erase a failing backend’s contribution. First distinguish a routed search, default-only search, and aggregate-root search.

No assumed POSIX mount semantics: aggregation includes backend-returned entries plus route entries. It does not imply mount-shadowing or deduplication, and it does not migrate default keys that happen to share a mounted-looking prefix.

sections.title: Execution always belongs to the default backend
sections.body:
CompositeBackend.execute never parses commands for mount prefixes. Sync and async execution delegate only to a default implementing SandboxBackendProtocol; otherwise they raise an unsupported-execution error.

Keep three boundaries separate

  1. File routing does not route shell commands. A shell backend mounted only at /remote/ does not enable execution through that route. A sandbox default plus a store at /memories/ still runs commands in the sandbox, whose OS filesystem does not automatically contain store documents.
  2. Transfers are grouped, then reordered. Bulk upload/download groups requests by backend, tracks original indices, calls each batch API, and reconstructs responses in original order with original paths. Group processing is sequential, including async variants—not automatic concurrent fanout. Custom backends must return one response per input; the missing-response fallback can leave error=None, so malformed short responses are not robust success guarantees.
  3. Aggregate deletion support is not universal route support. The composite advertises deletion because it implements the method. A route can still lack it; the composite catches that route’s NotImplementedError and returns a structured deletion error.

Illustrative failure mode, not executed: writing /memories/preferences.txt through a store route, then executing cat /memories/preferences.txt, can target different systems. A shared path string does not bridge them. Use file tools or explicitly transfer bytes into the execution environment first.

title: Remote execution, native adapters, and Context Hub commits
kicker: One interface, several transport and durability contracts
summary: Trace BaseSandbox command helpers, source-side output capture, LangSmith native transport, partner-specific failure behavior, and ContextHubBackend optimistic commit processing.

sections.title: BaseSandbox turns execution into structured file operations
sections.body:
BaseSandbox supplies structured file helpers for a provider that already offers execution and byte transfer. Subclasses provide execute, upload_files, download_files, and an identifier; commands and server-side scripts implement listing, reads, search, globbing, edits, and deletion.

Read the helper mechanics in three parts

  1. Read windows are selected remotely. A server-side Python script receives line-window arguments, limiting text crossing the provider boundary. Rendered output has a further roughly 500 KiB cap; binary data uses base64 rather than text slicing. Async helpers call aexecute, not invariably a thread around sync file methods, so a subclass can centralize native async transport.
  2. Writes have a preflight and a transfer. A command creates parents and validates the destination, then the subclass upload receives UTF-8 bytes. Empty upload responses cause assertion failure; reported upload errors become WriteResult.error. The source acknowledges a time-of-check/time-of-use window. Providers must honor their own parent-directory and error contracts; this distributed write is not atomic.
  3. Edits keep source files remote and reconcile line endings. Combined UTF-8 payload size selects an inline script or uploaded temporary old/new-string files. The edit script tries the original match and line-ending variants, transforming the replacement correspondingly. On mixed-ending files, replace-all affects the first matching style, not every normalized variant. This differs semantically from disk editing, not just in transport.

Authority is inherited: these helpers do not partition the underlying execution primitive. A caller can touch whatever the sandbox shell can reach.

sources.label: Edit payload dispatch and newline behavior

sections.title: Execution output: offloaded is not the same as truncated
sections.body:
Start with execution itself, then consider how much output can be returned. ExecuteResponse contains combined stdout/stderr in output, a possibly unknown exit_code, and a truncated flag. Output retention is separate from whether the command succeeded.

From command to result

Illustrative trace, not executed: assume a sandbox has /notes/brief.txt containing exactly Goal: summarize\n, and a successful cat command with no transport clipping. Its backend result can be:

response = sandbox.execute("cat /notes/brief.txt")
# ExecuteResponse(
#     output="Goal: summarize\n",
#     exit_code=0,
#     truncated=False,
# )

The filesystem execute tool packages command metadata in a ToolMessage.artifact. Its exit_code=0 describes command success. A command that ran and exited nonzero still has tool status “success”; validation that prevented execution instead has error status and no execution artifact. An unknown code proves neither success nor failure.

Then decide where large output goes

Illustrative capture settings: enable compatible source capture and call execute_with_offload with capture_path="/tmp/report-output.txt", max_inline_bytes=1024, and max_capture_bytes=8192. These are explicit example settings, not defaults. Assume no additional provider-side clipping.

Combined output emittedCapture resultWhat remains available?
512 bytesoffloaded=False, truncated=FalseComplete inline output
4096 bytesoffloaded=True, truncated=FalseInline preview; complete output at the capture path
16384 bytesoffloaded=True, truncated=TrueInline preview; only capped retained output at the capture path, with excess discarded

Offloaded means “look in this file for retained output.” Truncated means “some output was discarded.” Reading every page of a truncated capture file cannot recover the discarded part. A capture path is not unlimited archival storage.

Capture opt-in, completion codes, and trustworthy preview metadata
  • Source capture is opt-in. For compatible sandbox images, a wrapper retains large combined output in a sandbox file and returns a preview. The base flag defaults to false because compatible shell/core utilities are required. Without it, execution is unwrapped and generic eviction can occur after full output reaches the caller. LangSmith explicitly opts in; inheriting BaseSandbox does not.
  • Offload and truncation describe different facts. ExecuteOffloadResult.offloaded means output remains at the capture path; response.truncated means backend or capture limits discarded output. Offloaded contents may be complete or incomplete under the hard capture cap. Retained output is capped without killing the command, preserving its actual completion code.
  • Trust metadata, not marker-like output. Preview metadata explicitly records whether the wrapper inserted its middle-lines truncation marker. It does not infer that by searching output: a command can print the same marker. Untrusted output text must not become an execution-status or truncation control signal.

sections.title: LangSmithSandbox specializes transport and owns an async pool
sections.body:
The LangSmith adapter wraps an existing provider sandbox; its constructor does not provision one. The sandbox name is its ID, and default command timeout is 30 minutes.

Read the adapter contract in five parts

  1. Execution preserves the provider result. It calls run, joins stdout/stderr, preserves exit code, and sets truncated=False at this layer. That means the adapter applied no clipping; it is not independent measurement of every upstream transport.
  2. The async pool belongs to one event loop. Cached async client/sandbox objects avoid repeated connection pools and handshakes from converting the synchronous provider object. aclose clears and closes the pool. Repeated runs and loop churn must respect ownership: do not leak clients or reuse them across loops.
  3. Native transfer overrides the synchronous read/write path. Writes still run inherited parent preflight, then send bytes through the SDK. Nearby docstrings discuss older inline-shell writes, but the current base already delegates to upload. Follow the pinned call graph rather than historical rationale.
  4. Native reads classify and cap returned data. They fetch bytes, classify extensions, use base64 for invalid UTF-8 text, normalize line endings, and cap rendered pages. When a later boundary line is cut, resume normally advances only past complete returned lines. If the first line alone is too large, it advances one line for progress: that giant line’s unseen suffix can be lost in this preview interface.
  5. Transfer error codes are mappings, not diagnoses. Batches require a leading slash. Downloads map resource-not-found to file_not_found, and other sandbox-client errors heuristically to directory or missing-file codes. Upload client errors map to permission_denied. Preserve provider logs when authentication, transport, or permissions appear unusually categorized; the mapped code does not prove the remote cause.

sections.title: Partner adapters share helpers but not identical guarantees
sections.body:
Partner packages inherit structured helpers from BaseSandbox, but primitive transports differ materially. This is a source-level comparison, not a report of hosted-service exercises. Resource isolation, lifecycle, image contents, network access, and provider durability remain external responsibilities.

AdapterExecution pathTransfer / failure nuance
Modalexec("bash", "-c", command), wait, then read stdout/stderr; 30-minute default, zero waits indefinitelyNative sandbox file handles; known per-file filesystem errors normalized; handles closed in finally
RunloopDevbox command API; 30-minute default; output and exit mapped directlyDownload/upload loops do not catch per-file provider exceptions here; a failure can abort the batch
DaytonaPer-command session, asynchronous remote start, status polling, log retrieval under one deadlineNative batched transfers; upload API exceptions are not normalized per file here
VercelDetached bash -lc; wait thread implements caller timeout; best-effort killPer-file download mapping; valid uploads submitted as one batch and receive a shared batch failure

Three operational differences to keep visible

  1. Daytona budgets the whole execution path. Session creation, command initiation, polling, and logs share one monotonic deadline. Timeout returns code 124, with one shared two-second best-effort cleanup budget for partial logs and session deletion. Each request uses remaining time, accounting for SDK timeout rounding and an added request buffer. Zero disables the deadline; bounded cleanup attempts and warnings do not prove resource removal.
  2. Vercel timeout cannot directly cancel the SDK wait. A daemon wait thread is joined for remaining time. On expiry, a kill is attempted and code 124 returned; a failed kill warns the command may continue and incur cost. If completion succeeds but log fetching fails, the exit code is retained with an explicit output-unavailable message. The output ceiling is named in bytes but slices Python string length—not precise UTF-8 bytes.
  3. Retry only with side effects in mind. Timeout or transfer exceptions can follow successful effects whose responses were lost. Blind retries can repeat commands or uploads. The base asks for per-item partial success, but Runloop and Daytona show why concrete adapters must be inspected: the abstraction does not automatically enforce every transfer guarantee.

sections.title: ContextHubBackend is a versioned text tree, not an execution sandbox
sections.body:
ContextHubBackend stores files in a versioned LangSmith Hub agent repository, with no execution capability. Think of mutations as proposed commits against a known parent version, not as shell writes. If another writer commits first, the adapter must reload and reconsider the accepted operation.

Why a conflict replays intent

Illustrative trace, not executed: your cached /notes/brief.txt contains Status: draft Owner: Ada . You request an exact edit from Status: draft to Status: ready. Meanwhile another writer changes only the owner to Lin and commits first.

  1. The initial push conflicts. Your push names the old parent commit, so it cannot simply replace the newer tree using its stale materialized file.
  2. Reload and reapply the edit request. The adapter fetches Status: draft Owner: Lin and reruns the exact replacement. The new proposed content becomes Status: ready Owner: Lin : it preserves the other writer’s owner change because the edit still matches.
  3. Reject an intent that is no longer valid. If the refreshed file no longer contains Status: draft, replay fails rather than blindly writing your cached full file. A plain write differs: its intent retains the supplied value, so it is not an automatic merge of authors’ text.

How queued mutations become durable

A cold pull caches ordinary files as strings and records linked agents/skills separately; a missing repository is empty. Reads strip a leading slash, use the visible cache, and create fresh file-data metadata before slicing—not preserved remote creation history.

  1. Load the base tree and accept intent. Pull/cache the tree and parent commit when needed. Under one condition lock, validate edits against the visible tree and enqueue a mutation with intent, materialized changes, optional occurrence count, and completion event.
  2. Expose accepted changes while batching. Reads overlay in-flight and pending mutations on confirmed cache. A 50-millisecond window combines nearby writes into one push. Visibility is not yet durability: a successful write waits for its completion event rather than returning just after enqueueing.
  3. Push with optimistic concurrency. Merge a batch and push with parent_commit. On conflict, reload the remote tree, rematerialize edits and deletes in accepted order, and retry up to three conflicts beyond the initial attempt.
  4. Reapply intent, not stale edited contents. A write retains its supplied value; an edit reruns exact replacement on refreshed content and fails if invalid; deletion recomputes the refreshed subtree. Pending edits can be rejected even if the in-flight batch remains replayable.
  5. Settle every waiter. Success updates cache/commit identity, clears in-flight entries, and wakes waiters. Burst failure clears speculative state, invalidates cache, and settles affected waiters with the error. This includes unexpected worker exceptions.

Text-transfer limits: only UTF-8 is accepted. Undecodable uploads get invalid_path despite encoding being the actual issue. Duplicate upload paths are last-write-wins within a batch.

Search semantics differ: glob uses the shared matcher; grep includes use normalized fnmatch, where * crosses slashes. Grep’s path test is a raw prefix, so /foo can include foobar.... Use narrow canonical paths; do not assume grep and glob select identical sets.

title: Permissions, approval, and the real security boundary
kicker: Policy is a tool-layer gate, not universal authorization
summary: Derive first-match decisions, exact versus bulk approval, recursive-delete exceptions, execution limitations, and prompt-trust boundaries from current implementation and regression evidence.

sections.title: Read and write rules: ordered, default-allow, and path-sensitive
sections.body:
Filesystem permissions govern built-in file tools, not every way an agent can access data. Their operation type has exactly two values: read and write. Listing, reading, globbing, and grep are reads; writing, editing, and deletion are mutations. There is no filesystem-permission execute scope.

Use one policy throughout this lesson

Illustrative configuration, not executed: use a file-only backend, with SDK approval wiring for interrupt rules. The following order deliberately permits the exact report, asks about review drafts, then denies other notes writes. The final rule protects private reads.

from deepagents.middleware.filesystem import FilesystemPermission

permissions = [
    FilesystemPermission(["write"], ["/notes/report.txt"], "allow"),
    FilesystemPermission(["write"], ["/notes/review/**"], "interrupt"),
    FilesystemPermission(["write"], ["/notes/**"], "deny"),
    FilesystemPermission(["read"], ["/notes/private/**"], "deny"),
]
Ordinary requestFirst applicable decision
Read /notes/brief.txtNo matching read rule: allow by default
Write /notes/report.txtRule 1: allow, despite the later matching deny
Write /notes/review/report.txtRule 2: interrupt eligibility, not the later rule 3 deny
Write /notes/private/report.txtRule 3: deny
Read /notes/private/key.txtRule 4: deny
Write /scratch/report.txtNo matching write rule: allow by default

This is not a complete allowlist. Merely listing allowed paths leaves unmatched paths accessible. A restrictive allowlist needs specific allows before an appropriate catch-all deny, while accounting separately for recursive deletion.

How an ordinary decision is made

  1. Validate rule patterns. FilesystemPermission contains operations, absolute path patterns, and allow/deny/interrupt mode. Patterns must start with a slash, reject parent-directory components after separator normalization, and reject standalone tilde components. Matching uses wcmatch brace expansion and globstar support.
  2. Select the first applicable rule. Scan declaration order, skip other operations, and return the first matching mode; no match means allow. A later deny does not override an earlier allow on a direct read or edit.
  3. Check requested and resolved paths. Wrappers normalize paths. For filesystem backends, a deny on either the requested path or symlink-resolved target blocks; resolution failures count as denied. Composite mounts resolve in the routed backend and remap into composite coordinates.
Ordinary precedence at a glance
Ordered matches for one operation and pathOrdinary result
No matching ruleAllow
Allow, then denyAllow
Deny, then allowDeny
Interrupt, then denyInterrupt eligibility; denial is not selected by that later rule
Requested path allows, resolved alias target deniesDeny through resolved-target check

Custom output must be canonical: listings and matches need canonical absolute paths. Filtering compares returned strings against absolute rules; relative or noncanonical output can bypass intended filtering.

Enforcement is at the tool boundary: middleware.permissions is only a compatibility re-export. Enforcement lives in FilesystemMiddleware, not backend methods. Direct backend.read, user tools, and middleware reading through a backend do not automatically inherit these rules.

sections.title: Bulk read filtering and recursive deletion are special cases
sections.body:
Ordinary first-match decisions answer “may I touch this path?” A recursive deletion asks a wider question: “could anything removed below this path be protected?” Bulk discovery has another concern: which returned paths may the model see?

Apply the same notes policy to deletion

Illustrative trace, not executed: suppose /notes/report.txt is a confirmed plain file with no descendants, and /notes contains that report and the brief.

  • Delete the plain report: ordinary write precedence applies. Rule 1 allows its exact path even though rule 3 later denies /notes/**.
  • Delete the notes directory: the recursive check considers every overlapping deny-write pattern, regardless of earlier allows. Rule 3 blocks removing the subtree. Permission to remove the report does not authorize removing everything around it.
  • Do not infer “leaf” from one exact key. Flat state or stores can contain both /notes/report.txt and /notes/report.txt/attachment. The latter makes deletion potentially recursive despite the file-like name.

For discovery under the same policy, private read results are filtered out. This controls returned visibility; it does not promise that the backend never scanned denied bytes internally.

Discovery root prechecks and filtering
  • Filter discovered paths after discovery. Listing, globbing, and grep remove denied entries or matches, including resolved-target checks where supported. Interrupt-mode paths remain visible because approval happens earlier; hiding them afterward would silently remove data the user authorized.
  • Use the tool’s actual root precheck. Glob authorizes explicit path or omitted-path /, then filters matches. A pattern mentioning an allowed directory cannot bypass a catch-all deny on root: supply an explicit allowed path and relative pattern. Explicit-path grep checks its root; pathless grep can skip that precheck and filter later. Stores may load an entire namespace before filtering.
How conservative recursive-delete detection works

Listing probes distinguish a known leaf from a directory or ambiguous result. Known plain-file deletion uses ordinary first-match write precedence. If descendants may exist, every overlapping deny-write pattern is considered, even after an earlier allow. Empty directories remain conservative.

Literal patterns protect ancestor and descendant overlap; wildcard logic conservatively rejects possible protected descendants while permitting unrelated siblings. Regression assertions allow an exact workspace file despite a later catch-all deny, but block broader recursive directory deletion. Inspect overlap and leaf detection rather than only reordering rules.

sections.title: Interrupt rules are compiled into scope-aware HITL predicates
sections.body:
An interrupt asks a human to decide before a tool executes. FilesystemMiddleware enforces denies but does not itself pause execution. At graph construction, the SDK compiles interrupt-mode permissions into LangChain HumanInTheLoopMiddleware (HITL) configuration. Standalone filesystem middleware needs equivalent approval integration, or agent construction that wires the HITL layer.

Follow an approved write, including edited arguments

Illustrative trace, not executed: keep the notes policy from the first section and request a write to /notes/review/report.txt.

  1. Find the effective decision. Rule 2 selects interrupt before rule 3’s broader deny. With generated SDK HITL configuration intact, this exact write is eligible for an approval pause.
  2. Let the human choose a decision. Generated approvals offer approve, edit, reject, and respond. Approving permits the proposed call to proceed through its normal tool checks; responding skips execution.
  3. Recheck the actual final arguments. If the human edits the destination to /notes/private/report.txt, the write wrapper checks that destination, selects rule 3, and denies the call. Approval of the earlier destination does not bypass deny checks on edited arguments.

The SDK passes the decision contract to its dependency; it does not implement the entire human UI or durable resume transport. Nor should an application treat an approval prompt as proof that the eventual call is valid.

Exact and bulk approval predicates
  • Exact tools use ordered path decisions. Read, write, and edit normalize the named file and evaluate requested/resolved candidates. Approval fires if at least one decision is interrupt and none is deny. A denied symlink target suppresses an unnecessary prompt because the tool will reject it. Malformed paths do not prompt; later path validation rejects them.
  • Bulk tools use conservative subtree overlap. For ls, glob, grep, and delete, the predicate precomputes literal anchors before wildcard portions of interrupt patterns. It checks whether the requested subtree can overlap an anchor. Missing paths fire for any relevant interrupt rule. Current-directory aliases ., empty string, and ./ collapse to root so they cannot evade approval.
  • Conservative scope can over-prompt. A fully unanchored pattern such as /**/secrets anchors at root and can prompt on unrelated bulk calls. This tests reachability, not exhaustive actual matches or exact first-match precedence for every descendant. Glob separately checks its pattern: a harmless explicit path cannot hide an absolute protected pattern. Relative parent components also trigger approval conservatively, even if matcher validation later rejects them.

Approval is not validity or durability: configure the application’s LangGraph checkpointer and thread handling for durable pause/resume. A permission rule alone does not provide suspended-run storage.

sources.label: Final write arguments checked before backend mutation

sections.title: Overrides, subagents, and the execute gap
sections.body:
Approval policy follows the actual executing agent and tool boundary. Inheritance, replacement, and shell authority can all change what a parent-level rule appears to promise. Inspect the effective configuration, not just the original permissions list.

Explicit False disables prompting, not denies

Illustrative override, not executed: keep the notes policy but supply interrupt_on={"write_file": False}. User entries replace generated entries by tool name; they are not combined with the generated predicate.

  • A write to /notes/review/report.txt no longer pauses on its generated interrupt rule. The interrupt permission is not independently enforced as a pause after replacement.
  • A write to /notes/private/report.txt still encounters rule 3’s tool-level deny. False is not an authorization bypass; it only changes the approval layer.
  • Custom interrupt entries can likewise broaden or narrow prompting. Review them alongside filesystem rules rather than assuming both sets of predicates run.

The narrow CompositeBackend execution exception

Filesystem permissions plus an execution-capable backend normally raise NotImplementedError. The exception accepts a composite only when every rule’s pattern string starts with a configured route prefix. It checks strings—not shell text, physical mount accessibility, or proof that routes are inaccessible to execution.

Illustrative configurations, not executed: assume a valid execution-capable sandbox default and a separately configured store_backend, wired as CompositeBackend(default=sandbox, routes={"/memories/": store_backend}). The table describes the middleware’s permission-configuration guard, not a shell confinement test.

Permission paths, in an otherwise valid nonempty rule listGuard resultReason
["/memories/**"]Accepted by the guardEvery pattern starts with /memories/
["/notes/**"]Rejected with NotImplementedErrorNo configured route prefix matches
["/memories/**", "/notes/**"]Rejected with NotImplementedErrorEvery pattern must qualify, not merely one
["/memories"]Rejected with NotImplementedErrorThe route prefix contains the trailing slash; this bare root does not start with it

Accepted route-scoped rules govern structured file tools while commands still execute on the default. They do not constrain the shell’s physical reach. Configure execute-tool interrupt_on and genuine runtime isolation; a host shell reaching routed files can bypass structured-tool denies. Custom network/database tools are likewise outside filesystem-path rules.

Subagent policy replacement and remote boundaries

Declarative subagents inherit parent permissions unless their own permissions field is present, replacing the entire list. Their explicit interrupt_on replaces inherited user configuration before permission-generated entries merge.

Precompiled and remote subagents do not automatically gain the parent’s internal approvals; configure their runnable or remote server. A parent approval setup is not automatically installed inside another executing agent.

Debug the effective policy in order

  1. Identify the executor and effective rules. Find the agent actually executing the tool and inspect its replaced or inherited permission list. Evaluate its first matching ordinary rule, then resolve aliases.
  2. Check scope and overrides before assuming protection. Account for bulk/delete semantics, inspect the final per-tool interrupt entry, and determine whether the operation bypasses these built-in tools entirely.

sources.label: Tool denies remain independent of HITL overrides

sections.title: Threat modeling from current code, not historical absolutes
sections.body:
The repository’s generated threat model targets an older commit and calls itself experimental and non-authoritative. Use it to locate concerns, then validate behavior against the current pin—not as a statement of current guarantees.

Read the trust boundary in four parts

  1. Separate historical claims from current code. The threat model describes a deprecated nonvirtual disk default; the current constructor defaults to virtual mode. It describes memory without sanitization or trust guidance; current formatting strips HTML comments and identifies memory files as data, not hidden instructions. Those old statements are stale at this revision.
  2. Limited preprocessing is not a prompt-injection firewall. Memory text still enters model context. Visible malicious instructions survive comment removal, which neither authenticates authors nor verifies claims. The prompt asks the model to prefer explicit user requests and verified evidence, but real enforcement needs narrow tool authority, correct backends, external isolation, and human review of consequential actions.
  3. Trace damage to real tool authority. One threat chain is poisoned repository content → misleading tool or memory context → model-generated command → permissive execution backend. State-only defaults cannot execute host commands by themselves; user tools or LocalShellBackend change that capability. Remote isolation depends on provider limits for credentials, mounts, egress, resources, and lifecycle.
  4. Make deployment choices at those boundaries. Derive namespaces from authenticated identity; keep host secrets out of workspaces; separate unrelated tenants into independently authorized storage and execution resources. Review approval overrides as code, retain machine-readable exit/truncation metadata, and never promise external rollback from a graph checkpoint. These are operational implications, not automatically provisioned SDK features.

Evidence limits: these chapters inspect pinned SDK/partner implementation and selected regression assertions. They do not certify hosted isolation, external LangChain HITL internals, provider authentication, filesystem race resistance, or production durability. Illustrative traces were not executed. Cited tests document intended behavior and regression expectations, not passing runs.
